content.thinking:
I'm planning out the proportions for an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike, working out realistic scale for the frame, raked front fork, handlebar height, and wheel sizes before building the model.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up a root frame joint with hinge joints for steering, front and rear wheels, swingarm, and kickstand, making sure each part explicitly binds to its bone rather than relying on nearest-joint guessing. I need to be careful with imports and API calls since I can't test as I go, keeping things tight and robust while aiming for bold, beveled shapes with clean panel lines and a strong accent color like orange.

For the color palette, I'm picking off-white body panels, navy and gunmetal tones, orange accents, chrome, rubber, and a cyan glow for headlight, taillight, and underglow details — keeping glow parts as flat unlit colors since painted surfaces can't actually emit light. I'm considering textured decal planes mapped onto the curved tank surface using a sweep-based decal placement, positioning them carefully near the tank's surface coordinates.

For paint style, I'm leaning toward a subtle countershading technique rather than toon shading, with lighter tones on top and cooler shadows underneath to match the smooth gradient look of the aesthetic. Now I'm laying out the actual geometry coordinates in meters, defining wheel positions and radii along the vehicle's length.

For the chopper's raked fork, I'm calculating the steering axis angle and working out where the head tube and front axle land given a 34-degree rake and fork length, solving for the z-position so the geometry lines up correctly with the front wheel placement.

For the steering joint, the hinge rotates about bone +Y, matching the steering axis correctly. For wheels, I want the spin axis across the body, so setting joint direction along X means bone +Y aligns with X, letting rotation about bone Y produce the wheel's spin.

Now I'm laying out the full joint hierarchy: a root frame joint, a steer joint hinging off the frame, a front wheel joint hinging off the steer, and a swingarm joint hinging off the frame near the rear pivot for the rear suspension, with the rear fender fixed directly to the frame like a hardtail setup.

Actually, going hardtail: skipping the swingarm and parenting the rear wheel directly to the frame, since that's more authentic to a chopper. I'm settling on a joint set of frame, steer, wheelF, wheelR, a kickstand hinge, a throttle grip hinge, a clutch lever hinge, and a brake pedal hinge, giving roughly 8-10 joints, and checking whether the kickstand should reach the floor or if the bike stands fine on both wheels alone.

I'll keep the kickstand folded up near the rear left, angled so its tip sits just above ground level rather than clipping through the floor, and skip adding a rider since this is a vehicle-only model, though I might add a leather seat. Now I'm starting to lay out the frame component as a backbone tube swept from the head lug down to the seat post area, giving it that sloped chopper silhouette.

Next I'm working out the down tubes and double-cradle lower rails, routing them from the head down to the engine mount, along the bottom, and up to the rear axle dropouts, with upper seat stays running rigidly back to the same rear mounts. Then I'm positioning the V-twin engine at the frame's center, building the crankcase as a box with two angled cylinders splayed forward and back to form the V, each with cooling fins.

Now I'm thinking about how to construct the fenders and crankcase shapes using extrusions, lofts, and sweeps -- extruding bevelled profiles for the crankcase, and sweeping a thin elliptical cross-section along an arc path over the wheel to form each fender.

For the rear fender, I'm defining the arc's center as the wheel hub and computing the "from" point at radius 0.40, positioning it so the arc sweeps from roughly 50° above horizontal at the front over the top down to about -20° behind the wheel.

I'm reasoning through the rotation direction about the X-axis to determine which way the arc sweeps, settling on starting at roughly -110° (behind, slightly below horizontal) and rotating toward +40° (forward and up) to carry the arc from the rear over the top to the front.

Now I'm working out the front fender geometry, deciding whether to include a small skinny fender attached to the fork, spanning an arc around the wheel center from roughly 10° to 110°.

I'm also setting up the fat rear tire using a lathed profile around the X axis, defining radius and width parameters to get a rounded tire shape.

I'm planning the wheel assembly: a lathed dark rubber tire, a chrome rim ring, a hub with thin rod spokes radiating outward, an orange hub cap, and possibly a thin lathed disc for the brake rotor.

Instead of modeling rotor holes geometrically, I'm thinking of applying a drilled/mag-wheel pattern as an SVG texture onto circular planes placed on both faces of the wheel, using alpha transparency so the pattern reads consistently from either side.

I'll pair that texture with simple 3D elements like a chrome hub lathe and rim lip for depth, then sketch out the tank shape as a teardrop profile sweeping along the bike's spine with varying radius for a tapered look.

Tuning the radius curve...

I'm thinking through the tank's shape with the wide round bulb toward the front tapering back toward the seat, then planning the paint scheme as a two-tone countershade with an orange stripe band running along the sides.

Still defining paint palette...

Thickness constant 0.3 with 0.03 bevel and smoothing 1. I need to watch out for self-intersecting outlines when extruding, so I'll keep smoothing low and avoid overly complex polygons that risk crossing edges, accepting some risk on riskier shapes while using sweeps for fenders instead. For the engine, I'm planning a crankcase extrusion at 0.22 width with V-cylinders modeled as frustums.

For the cylinders I'm lathing a finned profile with alternating radii along tilted axes at roughly ±35° from vertical, giving a finned look for the rod sections. I'm adding rounded cylinder heads with lathe caps, orange rocker cover boxes, and dual chrome exhaust pipes on the right side (negative X) that sweep back from the exhaust ports using catmull curve points, tracing out from each cylinder head toward the rear with a heat shield along the way.

I'm defining the two exhaust pipes as staggered curves -- the front cylinder's pipe running lower and the rear cylinder's pipe running higher -- flaring out to wider tips with tapered radius and dark cap interiors, plus a slightly oversized perforated-looking heat shield segment over part of the pipe.

Now I'm working out how the engine connects to the frame: placing the tilted cylinders symmetrically front and rear from the crank center, computing their head positions, and leaving clearance below the tank before adding a round air cleaner housing to the side.

I'm fleshing out the air filter as a lathe disc with a chrome/orange ring, then adding the primary belt cover and gearbox housings on either side of the engine, plus the headlight glass in cyan-white, the tail light in orange-red, and deciding to keep orange as the dominant accent color while reserving cyan glow for small details like the headlight and underglow strips.

I'm setting up vector math helpers to compute points along the steering axis for the triple tree and ape-hanger handlebars, defining the rake direction and a function to place bar points relative to the steering head position.

Still plotting handlebar curve...

Now I'm placing the clutch lever joint on the left side, parented to steer with a hinge role, then adding a brake lever joint on the right. I'm also positioning the headlight as a round lathe shape at the front of the steering fork, between the fork legs.

Next I'm placing a small round speedometer gauge on the top clamp, using a textured circle facing the rider, before starting on the fork tube legs symmetrically on either side.

Still adding fork details...

Adding triple trees, then the front wheel axle, fork legs, disc brake caliper, and moving on to the rear wheel bone with its brake and belt drive setup.

Working out the belt/chain geometry between front and rear sprockets, computing top and bottom rod positions based on sprocket radii and wheel centers.

I also need to check clearances: the rear tire's width and the frame dropout positions could clash with the sprocket location, so I'm nudging the sprocket inward and widening the dropout spacing to keep everything from overlapping.

Now I'm sizing the rear fender to clear the fat tire, then shaping the solo seat pan's outline as a series of curved points from front to rear.

I'm realizing the seat bottom would overlap the backbone tube at that position, so I need to raise the seat slightly. I'm mapping out the backbone path from the head area down through the frame to the rear axle plate, treating it as a hardtail design where seat stays branch off to the axle.

Now I'm thinking about adding seat spring details using a spiral sweep for the coils, positioned near the front nose of the seat for that classic chopper look, and considering whether to add a tall sissy bar at the rear.

I'm figuring out the sissy bar silhouette, running from the seat area up and back for that heroic chopper look, with a small backrest pad across it, plus a rear fender strut and tail light mount. I'm calculating the fender's end angle so the tail light lens sits properly at the back, adjusting the arc to around -100 degrees so it doesn't end up too low.

Now I'm placing the tail light glow at the fender tip and working out a license plate texture with a non-trademarked placeholder text. I'm also laying out the forward foot controls with peg positions and a brake pedal hinge on the right side.

Still adding mechanical details...

I'm using a surface raycast to find where the cap should sit on top of the tank, then attaching a small cylinder there using the stick helper, rigged to the frame bone. Actually, placing the part directly at the computed position might be simpler than using stick.

For the decals, I'm figuring out placement on both sides of the tank using directional projection, with mirrored orientation for the side facing left versus right.

I'll size the tank decal around [0.46, 0.2] given the tank's dimensions, and plan to use SVG decals and painted lines for panel details, including an orange stripe on the rear fender using the surface coordinate.

Thinking through the color blocking for the tank: a white upper body with navy on the lower half and a thin orange center stripe bordered by navy, applying paint based on surface normal and position to separate base colors from the stripe.

That stripe band works fine across the tank's caps and ends. Now I'm thinking through the rest of the color scheme: fenders getting navy with an orange center stripe, frame and engine in gunmetal, chrome pipes, and a dark seat with orange piping along the edges for accent.

Adding seat piping curves...

Now I'm planning small bolt/rivet details—rim bolts, fork pinch bolts, crankcase bolts—using a merged sphere geometry helper, importing BufferGeometryUtils from the three.js addons path to batch them efficiently.

Still writing bolt helper...

I'm confirming the Joint type import from the skeleton module and deciding to keep everything scoped inside a build() closure. Now I'm setting up geometric constants like the rake angle and its cosine for the upcoming coordinate calculations.

Computing axle positions along the steer axis, checking that front and rear wheel radii properly meet the ground plane at y=0.

Now I'm sketching the overall chopper dimensions — roughly 2.65m long and 1.35m tall given the fender, fork, and sissy bar placement, which fits a long-fork chopper proportions. I'm starting to design a wheel-building function that takes a bone, center point, outer tire radius, width, and rim radius, beginning with the lathe profile points for the tire's cross-section.

Still writing tire profile...

Adding sidewall stripe logic...

Bumping paint resolution to 2048 for crispness, then working out the rim geometry — a lathed chrome ring sitting inside the tire bead radius so the sidewall and visible rim lip overlap correctly without clipping.

I'll give the rim a chrome-ish flat color, then work out where to place the wheel face disc axially so it sits inside the tire's inner hole without clashing with the sidewall geometry.

I'm setting up two circle planes facing outward on each side, sized to fit inside the hole radius, so only the front face of each is visible from its respective side while the texture retains its own coloring.

Now I'm sketching the hub geometry as a lathe profile for the chrome center, with a tapered outline revolved around its axis to match the wheel's depth, plus a separate orange dome cap lathed similarly for the center cover.

For mirroring across both sides, I realize flipping the outline's y-coordinates directly risks reversing the winding and causing culling issues, so instead I'll keep the same outline and flip the axis direction itself for the opposite side, which rotates rather than reflects the geometry.

Looking at the hat example, the outline moves from the axis outward along the bottom, up the outer edge, and back along the top — a counterclockwise path in (radius, axial) space. I'll apply that same convention to my tire outline too: starting at the lowest axial point, sweeping outward and up, then returning along the top.

Confirming the frame is right-handed, then I'm designing the brake rotor as a thin lathed disc with a drilled-hole texture using an svg ring pattern for the visual detail, planning dark steel coloring on one visible face.

I'll simplify: just a disc with a textured plane overlay showing the holes, skip spoke detail since the magnet already reads well, and add six small bolt spheres around the hub for extra realism. Now moving on to writing the fork details, being careful with the API types given how long this code is getting.

Checking the rod and sweep function signatures for passing colors and bone attachments, confirming Fill accepts a string or Paint object, and noting that smoothing curved sweeps needs catmull-interpolated points. I'm also weighing whether to lower the default sweep side count to keep triangle counts manageable for thinner tubes.

Now I'm sketching the overall build function structure, deciding which imports from the builder, skeleton, path, and paint modules are actually needed, and setting up metadata and a flat color palette for the model.

I'm defining countershade paint functions for white, navy, orange, and gunmetal surfaces, pairing light and dark tones to give each material a sense of depth.

Setting up the joint hierarchy...

I'm computing the kickstand's pivot-to-tip direction for its folded resting position, then defining the hinge joint and foot pad geometry. Now I'm working out the grip and triple-tree clamp coordinates before locking down the handlebar's overall geometry.

Mapping out riser rods from the clamp up to the bar, then plotting the symmetrical catmull curve points that form the bar's sweep across both grips, chrome-tubed around the steering bone.

Clutch lever pivots forward from the grip with the tip extending out and slightly down, mirrored for the brake lever on the right side. For mirrors, I'll use flattened spheres scaled down on one axis to approximate round mirror glass on short stalks.

Adding mirror stalks and speedo housing...

Normalizing that direction gives the actual face position offset from the gauge mount. For the gauge dial texture, I'm planning glowing orange arcs, a needle, tick marks, with the background kept dark so the glow pops. Now I'm working out the headlight placement, sizing its housing radius to fit snugly between the fork legs without clipping them.

Checking clearance between the headlight bucket and fork leg edges, then computing the headlight's center position by projecting forward along the steering axis and offsetting perpendicular to it in the up-forward plane. Writing lathe profile coordinates...

Adding a glowing cyan LED torus ring around the headlight bezel for a hero accent, then decorating the fork legs with orange ring decals, and starting on a front fender arc centered on the wheel radius.

I'm computing the fender sweep geometry spanning from behind-top to forward, with tapered ellipse cross-sections, then setting up support stays connecting the fender to the fork axle at both ends.

Checking whether the fork line actually clears the wheel: comparing fork z-position against the wheel's circular profile at the same height to see if the fork sits in front of or behind the tire surface near the top.

I'm checking whether the fender fits within the fork legs' inner clearance — the leg inner edge sits right at the fender's radius, so it's a tight but workable fit. Now I'm considering whether to add connecting stays between the fender top and the fork legs, but the geometry doesn't line up cleanly since the fender top and the nearest leg point are offset both horizontally and in height.

I'm now working through the rear fender geometry — checking radius, clearance against the tire, and the arc sweep from -100° to 45° to make sure the endpoints tie into the backbone region correctly. I'm also sketching out paint details for the fender (orange stripe) and starting to rough in the sissy bar's curve, basing its position off the fender top and seat stay attachment points.

Now I'm plotting the sissy bar as a mirrored catmull curve across both sides, chrome-finished, plus a small leather pad box near the top with dark coloring and orange trim accents.

For the pad placement, I'm positioning it at roughly (0,1.1,-0.875) so it overlaps the interior between the two bar curves. Then I'm figuring out where to mount the tail light near the rear of the fender, around φ=-85° to sit on top of the fender's curved surface.

I'm settling on placing the tail light near (0,0.33,-1.37) facing backward, using a small glowing red-orange sphere stretched into a lens shape with some glow intensity, plus thinking about adding brake light strips nearby.

Now I'm figuring out the license plate placement, trying to position a textured plane roughly at (0,0.27,-1.35) hanging vertically near the fender end, while avoiding overlap with the tail light above it by nudging the fender height slightly.

I'm thinking a slim LED bar shape would work better for the tail light, positioning it flush against the fender's curved surface at that rear angle.

Now moving to the engine, I'm placing the crank center and starting the crankcase profile as an extruded shape with a rounded block outline.

Now I'm setting up the cylinder geometry for the V-angle engine cylinders, computing axis directions for front and rear banks at 38 degrees and positioning their bases relative to the case, then starting to lathe the cooling fin profile along the cylinder length.

Building the fin outline point by point...

Still shaping engine details...

Mapping out the exhaust pipe route...continuing it down past the rear wheel, checking clearance against the tire and dropout, then starting the rear cylinder's exhaust path from its head face routed separately to avoid overlapping the front pipe.

Realizing the two pipe paths actually collide, so I'm staggering them -- shifting the front pipe to an outer x-lane and the rear pipe to a different height, like a two-tier drag-pipe setup, then tracing the front pipe's final coordinates down to its end point near the rear.

Still tapering the pipe...

I'll skip adding small clamp rings along the pipe path and instead focus on getting the tube radius and port position right, figuring out where the pipe should start relative to the head's surface geometry.

Now I'm placing the intake port near the front head, picking a start point slightly inside the head surface and routing the pipe outward and down. I'm also sketching the air cleaner housing as a lathe profile positioned between the cylinders.

Checking clearance between the air cleaner and the cylinder geometry -- computing where each cylinder's surface sits along the axial direction to make sure the housing doesn't collide with the front or rear cylinder at that y-position.

Now I'm working out the gearbox and primary cover details: a large chrome lathed disc on the right for the primary cover with an orange ring and bolt details, a smaller steel gear cover on the left side, plus a lathed sprocket and an orange inspection cap.

I'm shaping the engine mount plates on either side of the frame, sizing them slightly larger than the crankcase outline and defining their polygon shape to wrap around it cleanly.

Covers extend past the plates outward, confirming the side plates sit under the crankcase covers. Now I'm working out the plate extrusion parameters—thickness and bevel—plus starting the backbone tube path with a catmull spline curving down from the headstock.

I'm picking colors: navy frame with orange accent tubing, deciding the backbone and down tube routing from the head toward the engine. I need to check clearance between the down tube and the front cylinder head—routing through points near y=0.914 down to y=0.5, verifying the tube radius of 0.03 doesn't collide with the cylinder which spans out to roughly z=0.28 at that height, leaving about 0.065 clearance.

Checking the exhaust pipe routing against the down tube—the pipe sweeps from x=0 to x=-0.12 at a similar height, which comes too close to the down tube, so I'm adjusting the down tube path to bow forward more, ending near (0,0.40,0.24) to clear it. Then I'm laying out the cradle rails running from the down tube's end down and back along the frame, checking they don't intersect the crankcase, exhaust pipes, or rear pipe runs as they curve toward the rear.

Now I'm checking the swingarm rail against the belt drive—keeping the belt narrow and offset enough in x so the rail's inner edge clears it. For the seat stays, I'm routing them from the seat area down to the rear axle region, verifying they stay just inside the fender width without clipping the tire. I'm also noting the rear axle plate and dropouts need small extruded mounts near the axle caps.

Moving to the head tube, I'm placing it as a white rod along the steering axis with orange ring bands, and considering small gusset plates between the head tube and down tube (likely skippable for simplicity). For footpegs and forward controls, I'm planning a peg rod with a rubber end cap, connected back to the frame via a bracket rod running from the down tube area down to the peg position, making sure the reach relative to the front tire is reasonable.

Now I'm working out the brake pedal: a pivot joint on the frame with a pedal arm rod extending out to a pad box, set up as a hinge joint parented to the frame. The shift lever on the left side gets a similar rod-and-peg shape but stays fixed without its own joint, and I'm adding a rear disc rotor using a lathe-style radius function, plus considering cyan underglow strips along the lower frame rails near the engine.

Then I'm placing neon tube rods beneath the frame rails as glowing accents, adjusting their vertical position so they sit just under the rails without clipping through, and deciding to skip a cyan accent line on the tank itself. For the tank mounting, I'm sketching chrome strap bands that wrap around the tank using a closed curve fitted to the tank surface.

I'm a bit concerned about the loop potentially failing with no safety net for errors, but since crash recovery happens separately, I'll accept that moderate risk and focus on maximizing correctness rather than building in defensive checks.

Instead of relying on surface ray-casting, I decide to derive strap positions analytically from the tank's known path geometry — using the tank's centerline function and its radius functions at each point to construct ring points directly, which is much safer and avoids dependency on raycasting against the surface.

For the tank cap, I'm setting up a lathe-generated cylindrical cap with a chrome body and orange ring accent, positioned at the top of the tank along the Y axis.

Now I'm working out the tank's overall shape using a Catmull-Rom spline through a handful of control points, computing radius profiles along the path length with a sine-based taper for the tapering ends, and figuring out where the cap should sit relative to the tank's curvature.

Designing the tank decal SVG...

Still writing wheel SVG...

Writing coordinate rotation helper...

Writing wheel/tire geometry code...

Placing the front rotor at x≈0.085-0.092 as a lathed disc plus textured face, I'm checking it against the fork leg geometry at x=0.1 to see if they overlap near the axle region.

Realizing they'd intersect, I widen the fork leg spacing to x=±0.13 so the inner leg edge (0.102) clears the rotor's outer radius (0.0915), then start sizing the headlight housing around radius 0.08.

Now I'm checking the hub cylinder and end caps against the wider leg spacing to confirm the axle still passes through cleanly, and starting to position the caliper box relative to the rotor.

I'm working out where the caliper should attach along the leg, tracing the angled fork line to find the z-coordinate at a given height so the caliper sits correctly behind the axle near the rotor.

I'm placing a bracket rod connecting the caliper to the fork leg at the right point along its slope, then moving on to define the fork leg's stanchion segment with radius and chrome material.

Still working through the lower leg dimensions and planning orange accent bands and gaiter bellows, while figuring out where the axle attaches to the legs so I can move to designing the triple trees next.

Rod bands use ascending end-color pairs with flat caps by default. For the headlight mounts, I'm working out the geometry connecting the housing edges near the top to the fork legs below, offsetting forward so the mounting rods angle correctly toward the leg attachment points.

Fender stays are in place, and I'm adding seat springs, a kickstand, and skipping shocks since this is a hardtail design — just a spring under the seat. For decals I'll add a simple license plate text like "OVR-762" rendered with default font styling, then consider adding an oil tank or battery box near the seat area, though I may skip the oil tank since it's crowding the seat stay position.

Positioning the oil tank on the right side near the backbone, with careful placement to sit between the engine rear head and rear fender — then adding a battery box on the left with an orange strap, plus rubber hose sweeps connecting the oil tank to the engine using a curved catmull path.

Now I'm skipping spark plug wires and routing a throttle cable sweep from the right grip down past the tank to the carburetor, assigning it to the steering bone since it mostly follows the steering motion. I'm also planning the brake line sweep from the lever to the caliper.

I'll simplify to just a throttle cable and a steel-braided brake hose to the caliper, skipping footboards to keep the part count reasonable and triangle count well under budget.

Now I'm starting the SVG textures: a colored mag wheel texture, and a rotor texture with a steel ring and brake holes.

Writing the rotor path with evenodd fill rule...

Now moving to the gauge dial icon: a dark circular background with an outer cyan ring, tick marks sweeping 270 degrees with the last few highlighted orange, and an orange needle pointing from center.

Then I'm planning a license plate graphic with a rounded white-navy border, orange top stripe, and bold "RIDE-76" text, plus a tank decal at larger size, while skipping extra fender and seat stitching details.

Now I'm checking the transparency behavior for the SVG default background and thinking through the orange stripe placement on fenders before diving into the actual build code. I'm verifying the TypeScript types for the rod, joint, and part helper functions—making sure point arrays, color fills, and role unions all infer correctly before writing the full coordinate list.

I need to confirm the mergeGeometries import path resolves properly in the sandbox's typecheck setup, trusting the docs since they specify it explicitly. For the lathe function, I'm realizing the outline points need to be typed as tuples rather than plain number arrays, since the OutlinePoint type expects fixed-length tuples—so I'll need to annotate those literals explicitly to satisfy the type checker.

I'm checking potential runtime pitfalls, like whether a sweep radius function returning an array literal will cause a TypeScript tuple inference mismatch against the expected return type.

I'm also confirming the sweep overload signature with source, radius, color, and options, verifying that spike isn't needed, and checking that catmull accepts a point array with the closed option.

For the glow and lathe, I'm making sure the flat color is a plain string rather than a paint object, and checking the part call uses texture with a white color.

For the wheel geometry, I'm setting up circle discs for the rims with proper direction and axial offset for tire width, confirming that the visible plane from the viewer's side matches the correct normal direction.

Now I'm double-checking radius ratios between front and rear wheels against their plane sizes, worrying whether the disc planes might clip or z-fight with the rim lathe geometry since the rim is a closed solid spanning a radius and axial range that could overlap where the plane sits.

So that gives an inner rim lip, placing the plane radius at 0.58R, which sits inside the rim's inner radius and stays visible at the correct axial position. I'm now sketching the rim's lathe outline, tracing from the inner lip outward to the outer bead at 0.70R and back on both sides.

I'm checking that the chrome/white rim face overlaps correctly with the tire's inner radius so the bead reads naturally, and confirming the drawing plane is recessed behind the rim lip as intended. Part naming doesn't need to be unique, so I can move on.

Now I'm working out paint stripe placement for the fenders, figuring out how to define the stripe path along the rear fender's top center based on the x-coordinate.

For the stripe design I'm going with an orange center band flanked by thin white pinstripes, using axial distance thresholds to decide orange versus white versus the base paint color. Frame tubes get the base paint color while the engine gets its own shade, and I'm skipping extra detail like panel lines and decals for now to keep things simple.

Setting up rake angle and steering geometry constants...

Working out the forward-up vector perpendicular to the steering axis and verifying it against the headlight position math.

Defining front and rear axle points based on wheel radii, then starting to build out the joint list for the frame structure.

Adding the steer, front wheel, rear wheel, kickstand, throttle, clutch, and brake lever joints...

Still defining more joints...

Adjusting pivot coordinates to 1.245. Now I'm working out the handlebar riser geometry, figuring out clamp positions and the cross bar center placement for the risers connecting to the main bar.

Still placing geometry...

Setting up the build function and defining a color palette of hex constants for chrome, steel, gunmetal, navy, black, and rubber tones.

Defining shaded paint gradients...

Writing the wheel helper function...

Still writing the lathe shading logic...

Still defining hub geometry and cap lathes...

Still writing rotor geometry...

I'm now designing the fender builder function, figuring out radius, sweep angle, and color parameters, and sorting out the correct Fill type import for the color argument.

I'm weighing section shape for the fender tube—circle vs box cross-section—and deciding to keep a circular profile with more sides for smoother ellipses, while figuring out ring density based on turn angle per sweep segment.

Now I'm sketching out the helper functions for frame construction: a sweep-based tube helper for curved paths and a rod helper for straight segments, both taking points, radius, color, and bone binding. Time to write it all out, aiming for roughly 500 lines total while being careful with variable naming consistency.

For the engine, I'm defining cylinder bank geometry using a lathe profile with fins arranged radially around each cylinder, positioned and oriented along a direction vector so banks point forward and rearward at an angle.

Then I'm layering the head and rocker cap on top of each cylinder: the head lathe shape tapers out and in to form the valve cover contour, with an orange rocker cap nested slightly embedded into the head's top for a snug fit. I'm also planning a ring of chrome bolts around the head top for added detail.

Now I'm positioning the right engine cover disc, lathing a tapered plate shape and aligning its radius and center so it sits flush against the crankcase plates without poking outside their silhouette, plus adding an orange accent ring on the cover.

Adding bolts and inspection cap...

Still writing sweep geometry...

Still defining pulley geometry...

Skipping the guard, I'm setting belt x at 0.137 within the pulley range, placing the rear rotor and axle cap near x=-0.19, and checking that the seat stays running from the top tube down to the rear axle stay inside the fender's radius envelope without clipping it.

That path actually cuts through the tire itself at x=0.1 since the tire's half-width is 0.105, so I need to reroute: take the stay outward above the fender crown near y=0.70 where the fender top sits around y=0.684, swing it out past x=0.2 to clear the fender width, then angle back down to the axle point.

Checking the fender's extent—it only spans to about φ=45° (ending near y=0.619, z=-0.671)—so I'll connect two short strut rods from the seat stay to the fender's front edge for support. For the cradle rail beyond the fender zone, placing it at x=0.16-0.19 keeps it clear of the tire's 0.105 half-width margin.

For the seat, I'm spanning z from 0.05 to -0.66, positioned above the backbone and clear of the fender's rear peak. Checking bolt placement around the rear pulley ring and verifying the exhaust pipe route stays clear of the rear tire and rotor—pipe sits at x=-0.24 to -0.27, well outside the tire's 0.105 boundary and the rotor's -0.125 to -0.132 range.

The front and rear pipes clear the frame stays by just a few millimeters at their closest points near z=-0.95, so I'm confirming no actual overlap occurs. The seat bottom sinks slightly into the backbone tube, which is expected since the seat rests on top of it, and the tank-to-frame clearance checks out too.

Now I'm setting up a chrome saddle strap ring connecting the tank to the frame.

For the kickstand, I'm placing a steel pivot rod with a rubber foot pad, working out the pivot point by interpolating along the frame rail near z=-0.3 and positioning the tip so the kickstand swings naturally into contact with the ground.

But checking against the belt geometry, I realize the kickstand pivot rail at z=-0.6 actually overlaps the belt's position at x≈0.137, so I need to shift the cradle rails further outward to avoid the collision -- adjusting the rail path to curve out to x=0.19 earlier.

I'm trying to adjust the rail path so it clears the crankcase cover and pulley geometry, checking that the belt stays inside the rail boundary at each cross-section near the front pulley.

The rails run from the footpeg bracket area back toward the engine, and I'm verifying they clear the front engine plates without collision—checking that the rail radius plus plate thickness still leaves clearance.
